courses.actualProfile: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate student formation, namely, actively, consciously and ethically relating to oneself, others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhances critical thinking and independent learning. It also helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners. The course stimulates core academic skills, namely: Select and critically analyze academic sources Articulate research questions, thesis statements and arguments Improve communication skills through various forms of writing and speaking activities The course fosters personal, social and civic competencies, namely: Craft own academic and personal learning goals Critically reflect on own learning Develop effective collaborative learning approaches with peers, instructors and external partners Valuing community engagement, including the value of different knowledge types and perspectives

courses.actualProfile: This course offers three different perspectives on the law: the legal, the social and the normative. We spend the first part of the course exploring the definitions of law and the different understandings of law in a general sense. We take a brief look at the different legal systems of the world, and we discuss various fields of law: constitutional law, administrative law, criminal law, international law and human rights, as well as select fields of private law including property law, contract and torts law. After the Fall break, students consider the relationships between law and society and the concept of justice. In addition to reading and discussing the main principles within each field of law, we explore these through reading case law and performing trial simulations.
courses.description2: Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. Explores definitions, legal traditions and fields of law, investigates the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice, and includes case law, excursion to international legal organisations, interviews with practitioners and a moot court session.

courses.actualProfile: In the course Introduction to Political Philosophy we shall examine the views on the nature of man, of society, and of political authority held by a number of influential Western thinkers. By the means of their particular political theories, the thinkers in question certainly intended to contribute to the solution of problems affecting the communities they were part of and their time. We shall look at the intellectual presuppositions of their theories and compare the problems they intended to solve, as well as their solutions, with the most significant actual political problems, the perception the general public opinion has of them and our current solutions. In particular, we shall focus on the authors’ justification for the existence and organization of political power. The course aims to provide a comprehensive introduction to the nature, characters, and purposes of each of the various political theories examined, from classical antiquity to today. To achieve this goal it is designed as informative and critical. Students are expected to master a number of relevant items and to assess form and quality of the influence that certain political theories have had, and may still have, on present day politics. In the attempt to determine whether there are ‘perennial’ political problems and features, students are expected to constantly compare past and present, and to find out what are the possible connections between empirical and normative political science.
courses.description2: Introduces political philosophy. Examines concepts such as authority, freedom, equality, democracy, human rights, pluralism, multiculturalism, poverty and environmental issues through classical and contemporary texts. Emphasises essay writing and presentations.
courses.topics: political philosophy; emphasises essay writing; contemporary texts; presentations; poverty; pluralism
courses.finding: Political authority/theory from classical to contemporary thinkers; strong substantive political contribution.

courses.actualProfile: All over the world people seem increasingly dissatisfied with the way their political system works, whether its citizens in Bangladesh who ousted the Hasina government, or voters in consolidated democracies like Sweden who are increasingly voting for parties at the left and right extremes of the political spectrum. How can we understand and explain these developments? Foundations of comparative politics provides you with the key analytical tools to analyze and compare political systems and the development and functioning of democracies in particular. This is done using the research tools of ‘mainstream’ political science: theory driven qualitative and quantitative empirical research that seeks to describe and/or explain political phenomena. The course provides an overview and analysis of the core structures and institutions of political systems by examining the position of the state and studying its internal structures and functioning and its interaction with society. We examine these issues using the conceptual toolbox of comparative politics. We familiarize ourselves with the basic institutions that make up political institutions, and the way democracies and authoritarian regimes develop and can break down. We examine the functioning of consolidated democracies and the challenges they face from developments such as the decline of political parties, mediatization, the rising importance of non- majoritarian institutions such as courts and impact of globalization and internationalization on the capacity of domestic governments to act.
courses.description2: Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.

courses.actualProfile: This course introduces you to the European Union, a body politic that has been characterized as diverse as Unidentified Political Object, an unimperial empire as well as a superstate. Whatever its nickname , the EU is as political as any other body invested with public authority. For political scientists this means that it is vital to understand its functioning and to see where power is exercised and how various state and non-state interests try to get their preferences turned into policies. In the first part of the course we outline key actors, institutions and decision -making rules and show how political scientists have employed various ways to study EU politics and policy- making. Students will engage in Navigating the EU exercises that show them EU politics in the making and the sources to be used for that. In the second part of the course we will more directly examine the clash of interests through a group based research project where you study a legislative dossier and the interaction between interest groups and Members of the European Parliament, using the E Us transparency register . A key focal point in this analysis concerns the relative power of business interests vis a vis other interests in EU - decisionmaking and assessing what this implies for the legitimacy and effectiveness of EU - policies.
courses.description2: Introduces EU politics. Outlines actors, institutions and decision‑making rules; examines responses to crises; and employs various approaches to study EU politics and policy‑making.

courses.actualProfile: In this course on constitutional law and administrative law, students will undertake an exploration of the essential principles of these foundational legal fields. A comparative approach is used, examining and analyzing the constitutional law of five different legal systems. A constitution is the “fundamental and organic law of a nation or state that establishes the institutions and apparatus of government, defines the scope of governmental sovereign powers, and guarantees individual civil rights and civil liberties”, and ther efore, constitutional law is the “field of law dealing with aspects of constitutional provisions, such as restrictions on government powers and guarantees of rights.” (Blacks Law Dictionary 8 Ed, Garner et al eds, West 2004.) Yet, constitutional law is so much more than is suggested by these definitions. At the center of the modern constitutional state is the law, which protects peace, freedom and security. It is this law that is controlling, not the human actors in a state. In order that all may have acce ss to and rely on it, this law should be enshrined in a written document. Democracy demands a law that is enacted by a legislative body after public debate about its contents. The foundational values of a legal culture are written down in its constitution. The constitution takes up established values, tried and tested institutions and reliable political experience and passes them on to the next generation in a binding manner.
courses.description2: Explores constitutional law and state organisation, using a comparative approach. Covers constitutionalism, separation of powers, judicial review, federalism and fundamental rights, and discusses constitution‑making, religious constitutions and constitutional backsliding.
courses.topics: restrictions on government powers; guarantees of rights; constitutional law; comparative; religious constitutions; judicial review
courses.finding: Comparative constitutional/administrative law across five systems; direct law/governance contribution without equating all of BPSV/PublicManagement.

courses.actualProfile: EU law is everywhere, from the very strict new rules on data-protection that literally pop-up with every website you open, to less apparent instances such as the EU rules on reducing plastic bags that have found their way into distinct and different national laws throughout the EU. European law by now significantly affects the legal order in European countries and reflects as well as shapes the process of European integration in multiple ways. This course introduces you to the EU legal order by familiarizing you first with the institutional framework of the European Union and the organization of its legal foundations in particular. We will then survey the key substantive areas of EU law that revolve around EU fundamental rights, citizenship, and the freedom of movement of persons, workers, goods and establishments. You will be equipped to understand the EU legal order and research its manifestations both at the EU level as well as in the domestic context in which most of the EU law manifests itself in the lives of citizens, consumers, businesses and governments. There will also be guest lectures to further illustrate EU law and its functioning in theory and practice. The course is divided in two main parts. In the first part we will jointly examine the procedural aspects of EU law through a combination of brief lectures, in-class exercises and discussions. In the second part we will study the substantive law of the EU through the method of Problem Based Learning. Students will study a relevant case using the seven-step PBL method.
courses.description2: Introduces the EU legal order. Studies institutions, framework, citizenship and the internal market using problem‑based exercises and guest lectures.

The seco nd part of the course covers macroeconomics, beginning with an exploration of macroeconomics events and fundamental concepts such as aggregate output, unemployment and inflation rate. It then examines the dynamics of goods and financial markets in the short run.

Key indicators such as national income, economic growth, inflation, and unemployment are studied. The course analyses how fiscal and monetary polici es affect the economy. It also covers business cycles, economic crises, and international trade, providing the tools needed to interpret economic data, evaluate policy decisions, and understand global economic trends.

courses.actualProfile: This course provides a comprehensive exploration of advanced topics in microeconomic theory. Structured in three parts, the course begins with an in-depth analysis of consumer behaviour, including decision-making under uncertainty, non -egoistic preferences, and cognitive limitations. The second part analyses market structures with an emphasis on imperfect competition, strategic behaviour, and the functioning of factor markets. The final part of the course covers general equilibrium and market efficiency, investigating externalities and the role of government in the economy. Throughout the course, students will engage with research papers through presentations and discussions, bridging theoretical concepts with empirical evidence.

courses.actualProfile: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

courses.actualProfile: Research Methods & Statistics is a general introduction in research methodology and statistics. The introduction to methodology includes the logics and design of research (e.g., operationalization, experimental design, sampling), and some specific techniques (e.g., laboratory research, surveys). The introduction to statistics includes descriptive and inferential statistics, covering measures of central tendency, spread, association, univariate and bivariate inferential statistics, and analysis of variance. This course includes an introduction to simple applications of multivariate statistics but most coverage of multivariate statistics and statistical modelling will be covered in the course HCBPSYC211 Statistics & Experimental Methods in Health & Behavioral Sciences. The first 9 course weeks (not including the semester break) of the course provide the theoretical background. This includes not only instruction and practice in basic research methodology and statistics, but also the planning stages of the group research projects that will dominate the latter portion of the semester. In this portion of the semester, students of each section attend two classes each week with their instructor. Project groups are formed, and these groups work together in applying newly learned concepts to their own research problem thru individually completed homework exercises, and through sharing and discussing their progress with the rest of the class. The final 6 course weeks are dedicated exclusively to group project work. This research project can fall within any academic discipline.
courses.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.

courses.actualProfile: Sociology provides a diverse and intricate toolkit composed of concepts, methods, and theories, which aids in comprehending and dissecting the functioning of societies on a local scale and the complex interconnections triggering global phenomena. Unlike disciplines like economics or political science, the subject of sociological inquiry is less clearly de fined. It encompasses all facets of human engagement within society, spanning from everyday interactions to the most longstanding social institutions. As a result, the wealth of knowledge within sociology can feel daunting, leaving one uncertain about where to begin. The course follows the recommendations 3 of the Sociological Literacy Framework 1, which is composed of the essential concepts and competencies in the discipline, as portrayed in the following table: Furthermore, this course overviews some of the most impactful sociological theories, including those by Marx, Weber, Durkheim, and Du Bois. It recognizes the social and historical backdrop that shaped these “classical” sociological ideas and concepts, notably influenced by imperialism and colonialism. This historical context notably sidelined the voices of BIPOC (Black, Indigenous, and People of Color) and women. Consequently, fundamental concepts like race and gender received inadequate theoretical attention within “classical” sociology. To bridge this gap, the course will prioritize students ’ interests and intellectual needs.

courses.actualProfile: Similar to their quantitative counterparts, qualitative researchers ask basic, but demanding, questions before they start making any enquires, e.g. What is truth? What is reality? What is knowledge? Why do we want to conduct research? What do we want to get out of it? In contrast to quantitative studies, however, qualitative researchers are less interested in numbers, trends and generalisations. Instead, they are keen to explore the messiness of social processes: what motivates people to take actions, how people make sense of their world, and how politics, history and cultures influence people’s thinking and actions. In this course, we will critically examine the four key stages of conducting qualitative research: (1) research design and preparation; (2) data collection and management; (3) data analysis and interpretation, and (4) research dissemination. Throughout the course, students are expected to take an active role – to form a research group and choose a research topic, to interrogate qualitative research theories and their own research experiences, and to critically reflect the research processes and students’ own positionality, biases and assumptions. At the end of the course, students will share their research findings and experiences with one another.
courses.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.

courses.actualProfile: This course gives a chronological overview of history in the modern period (1815-2025). The nineteenth century saw the rise of industrial societies and of the new political ideals of popular sovereignty (e.g. Marxism, socialism) and national self-determination. These forces continued to operate in the twentieth century, which was characterized by tremendous upheavals like the Russian Revolution, the two World Wars and the demise of communism in Eastern Europe. The course offers a survey of the main economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present. Special attention will be paid to the relationship between economic developments and the international changes of the Balance of Power. A number of issues of seminal importance to modern history will be analysed thoroughly: the revolutions of the 19th century, the Belle Epoque, the origins of the First World War, the Great Depression, and the Second World War, the Cold War and the rise of the welfare state, the decolonization process, and the European economic and monetary co-operation between nations.
courses.description2: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.

courses.actualProfile: Tweets by politicians and celebrities. Social media conspiracy theories. Product advertising. Anti-war protests. Speeches about justice. These are all examples of rhetorical discourse. Both the internet and history books are full of examples of the relevance of the art of rhetoric, as are our daily lives. Plato defined rhetoric as the “art of enchanting the soul”, while Aristotle considered it the ability to “discover in any particular case, all of the available means of persuasion". Quintilian, on the other hand, simply considered rhetoric to be “the art of the good person speaking well”. Whatever the definition, mastering this art often involves more work than is often imagined; work that is at the core of this course. This course is a fundamentally a skills course, even if there is a significant amount of rhetorical history and theory. No effective standpoint can be formed, no supporting arguments found, no paper written, no presentation given, no textual analysis conducted without knowledge of how rhetoric works. Therefore, it is necessary for students to have a proper understanding of what rhetoric is and what it involves, and also how rhetoric can be applied consciously. This course offers the skills that students will need to be able to structure any future academic essay or future oral presentation in a clear, persuasive and academic way. courses.actualProfile: This third-year course on ‘persuasive communication’ in the connected realms of ‘science, society and sustainability’ will build on your existing knowledge of classical rhetoric and argumentation theory and look at persuasion mostly beyond the humanities in the fields of communication studies, social psychology and neuroscience. The course has several aims. The first is to make students aware of persuasion strategies that circulate in everyday social discourses. These discourses can be found in the domains of local politics, law, advertising, business, media and governmental institutions. Students will be introduced to new theoretical frameworks and models, such as framing, nudging, cognitive shorthands and the coactive model of persuasion. Simultaneously, they will learn about the importance of the ethics of persuasive communication in given public contexts. Ethical theories that we will explore will range from utilitarianism to universalism and from dialogic ethics to situationalism. The course will build towards a significant community engaged learning (CEL) element. This is the main aim of the course; namely, to get university students out of the classroom and into the real world of work and applied skills experience. This CEL aspect will mainly take place in the second half of the semester. Here, with their newly acquired persuasive communication knowledge and skills, students will help local institutions to address and solve both internal and external communication challenges that they currently have.
courses.description2: Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and energy.

courses.actualProfile: Our actions and decisions are structured by the ways we think about values, about what the good is. This course explores theories of moral reasoning, building upon historical and contemporary sources. In the first part of the course, we will examine the main theories in ethics – virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism – as well as questions pertaining to moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility, feminist contributions to ethical theory, the challenge of nihilism, and the relation of happiness and pleasure to ethics. The second part of the course largely focuses on practical ethics, touching upon topics such as equality, animal rights, poverty and wealth, future generations, climate change, historical injustice. We will examine our attitudes to these contentious and challenging issues, the way the topics relate to each other, and the manner in which questions in practical ethics highlight and bring into focus broader concerns pertaining to moral, political, and legal theory. Students taking the course will acquire in-depth knowledge of ethical theories, to be assessed through a mid-term exam. They will also work on developing research skills in papers and presentations, analyzing and assessing arguments from ethical theory and practical ethics while articulating an independent, informed perspective. Towards that end, throughout the term students will compose two reflection papers concerning topics in ethics, and in the second part of the term students will develop a research project comprising a final argumentative essay and a presentation.
courses.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. courses.actualProfile: This course provides students insights into the main legal issues in the fields of criminal law and criminal justice. We will discuss the concepts of criminal accountability, differentiated types of ‘guilt’, the essentials of justifications and excuse, the importance of the legality principle and other fundamental considerations, such as the ‘presumption of innocence’. Students are also introduced to interdisciplinary research into organized crime. The main guiding principles of criminal law and criminal justice will be presented and investigated and the moral and legal debate on the justification of punishment and on recent developments in criminal law will be considered. Special attention will be paid to legal skills, such as reading legal texts, analyzing criminal case law and formulating a normative opinion, based on legally and morally sound argumentation. Students apply theory and skills in a simulated legal aid clinic.

courses.actualProfile: This course serves as a general introduction to public international law as a field of study and professional discipline. Designed to provide you with a foundational knowledge of the creation and the historical evolution of the subject, it is broadly divided into three parts. The first part deals with general principles of international law such as its sources, subjects, and organization. In the second part, the focus shifts to specific domains, namely the regulation of the use of force, the law of armed co nflict, international criminal law, refugee law, and environmental law. The final part addresses the politics of international law as it delves into issues such as the right to self-determination, Third World Approaches to International Law, and questions of treaty negotiation, compliance and effectiveness. The general purpose of the course is to shed light on some of the most important questions of international law both from a formal legal and a social science perspective. Performance in the course will be assessed through in-class exercises, a preparatory and an open book exam, a podcast and a reflection report.

courses.actualProfile: Machine learning concerns an ever -expanding set of tools for understanding data and making predictions. This course introduces the fundamentals of machine learning. It presents several of the most important modelling and prediction techniques, along with several relevant applications. Topics include linear regression, classification, resampling methods, shrinkage approaches, tree - based methods, support vector machines, clustering, and more. Real-world examples are used to illustrate the methods, their strengths, and their limitations.

courses.actualProfile: In the summer of 1809 the British sailed some 40,000 soldiers and 5,000 horses in 500 navy vessels over the English Channel to land in Walcheren. This greatest amphibious operation in Napoleonic times became know as the Walcheren Expedition or the Expedition to the Scheldt. The ultimate British goal was to occupy the important harbour of Antwerp. On the other side, Dutch and French forces, including many foreign troops like Irish, German and Polish were trying to stop the British assault. The outcome of the Walcheren Expedition not only left a big mark on local history, but also had an enormous impact on the Netherlands, France, Great Brittain and international politics in general. In this course we will research the primary sources about the Walcheren expedition. Think about diaries, letters, memoirs and official reports written by soldiers, officers or officials form all participants in this conflict. You will learn how to search for, read and analyse these primary sources, through writing a course-filling paper; as such, this course will require a lot of self-study and fewer class meetings.
courses.description2: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.

courses.actualProfile: The Style and Meaning course is firmly grounded in stylistics, which is the study of style in texts. Stylistics involves identifying and analysing the linguistic choices that serve to create meaning in texts. Originally an outgrowth of the third canon of classical rhetoric (elocutio), and later heavily influenced by movements in twentieth and twenty-first century linguistics, modern stylistics has grown into a recognizable discipline in its own right, with its own distinct theories and practices. While stylistics can be used to analyse any type of text, traditionally the discipline has been most concerned with the style of literary texts. As such, stylistics has sometimes been referred to as ‘literary stylistics’ or ‘literary linguistics.’ The course textbook also works almost exclusively with fictional texts to introduce and illustrate theoretical concepts and frameworks and their application. Nonetheless, further in-class application will at times extend beyond the fictional and students will be allowed to choose non-fictional texts for their instruction presentations and term papers. Students will be invited to consider the linguistic choices made by (literary) writers by reflecting on why certain linguistic strategies may be more effective than others in achieving particular interpretive effects. Students will be asked to consider all levels of language from the phonetic to the discoursal, to the cognitive. Therefore, an interest in language is crucial to this course.
courses.description2: Explores how linguistic choices inform meaning and interpretation in literary and non-fiction contexts. Introduces theoretical frameworks for close reading and addresses power dynamics, obligation, uncertainty and ideological undertones in language.

courses.actualProfile: MCCMED111: Introduction to Film & Media provides you with a solid foundation in the study of film, while also introducing you briefly to media more broadly. The course begins by tracing the development of cinema from its earliest experiments to later artistic movements and innovations. This historical perspective helps you understand film not only as entertainment but also as an evolving cultural form that reflects and shapes society. At the same time, we focus on the elements of film form, such as narrative, cinematography, editing, and sound, which give you the vocabulary needed to describe and analyze how films work. Much of our attention is on film culture and analysis, since these provide the best starting point for further study in the field. Together, we examine and discuss influential examples, considering both their artistic qualities and their broader theoretical and political contexts. This approach allows you to see how films respond to social change while also experimenting with style and technique. In the final part of the course, we widen our perspective to take a short look at media more generally. By considering examples from television, streaming, and digital platforms, we make connections between film and the wider media environment and prepare the ground for more advanced courses in the cluster. Engagement with academic readings is another central part of the course. These texts present important concepts and debates that shape the study of film and media.
courses.description2: Introduces film and media as systems of meaning and cultural production. Examines how images, narratives and technologies shape perception, identity and power; covers film storytelling, representation and genres; and develops critical engagement skills.

courses.actualProfile: This course examines social history and everyday life through American mainstream media from the mid-twentieth century to the present. Its central premise is threefold. First, storytelling shapes how we understand the world. Second, who gets to tell the story matters. Third, media provides insight into the past, present, and constructions for possible futures. Engaging with narratives across a wide range of media, from television and film to podcasts and TikTok, supports this point. So does amplifying the voices of the silenced and treating viral moments, such as a Justin Bieber performance clip, as cultural snapshots that reveal contemporary values, anxieties, and desires. The course opens with fear, conformity, and identity, using The Twilight Zone (1959) and Black Mirror (2011–) as bookends of the same uneasy question: what does society do to the individual? Week two then draws from future foresight methodology to explore the question: what does society imagine for itself in the future? Who is centered and who left out of the imaginations? The course then turns to mediated constructions of "reality," placing competing versions of the same story side by side and asking who the narrative serves and who it harms. Case studies include the "Hollywood Indian" versus films written, directed, and acted by Native Americans. The juxtaposition exposes how the media both marginalizes and empowers. A parallel examination of disability representation contrasts the inspirational "disabled hero" trope with authentic portrayals by differently abled people themselves.

courses.actualProfile: Creative Communication Laboratory is an academic course that examines how meaning is produced through imagination, experimentation, and artistic practice. Creative work is studied and developed within a framework of critical reading, analytical discussion, and reflective writing. Communication is approached as a cultural and theoretical problem shaped by language, sound, rhythm, performance, and media. You will analyze how writers and artists use language to generate meaning beyond description, and how formal deviation operates as a deliberate, historically situated practice rather than error. The first part of the course focuses on poetry and performance as foundational practices. You will progress from traditional lyric forms to bent, strained, and experimental poetry, situating these practices within literary, historical, and cultural contexts. Class emphasizes rhythm, sound, imagery, voice, and embodiment, combining close reading with creative and analytical work. In this course, poetry is treated both as a genre and as a transferable set of strategies that cultivate formal control and precision. After Spring Break and the exam, the course turns to hybrid forms and independent creative projects. You will extend poetic methods into broader creative practices, including performative, sound-based, or digitally mediated work. Final projects may not involve singing, songwriting, or music performance, and sound-based work is permitted only when sound functions as a poetic, linguistic, or conceptual material.
courses.description2: Explores meaning-making through creative expression. Students study and practice poetic forms, experiment with sonic poetry, performance and other unconventional forms of communication, engage with theoretical texts and produce their own creative work.

courses.actualProfile: Developments in AI are transforming the nature of human interaction and raising fundamental questions concerning human flourishing and its alignment with technological progress. This course examines these issues from both philosophical and psychological pe rspectives, while exploring the deep connections between the two fields. In a module on the ethics of AI, we'll consider ramifications of the use of AI in the context of moral inquiry. Core topics include AI fairness and bias , privacy, responsibility and accountability . We will also approach the question concerning the moral status of AI systems , and some of the broader implications of AI, focusing on existential risks and broad political implications of the use of AI. In a module on psychology of AI, we will examine what it means to be human when AI systems increasingly mirror or simulate uniquely human capabilities. Research shows that people may both over-trust and resist AI in decision-making, which subsequently raises questions on responsibility and agency. In clinical and therapeutic contexts, AI challenges ideas of empathy, confidentiality, and the therapeutic alliance, while in organisational and social domains, algorithmic biases reflect and amplify existing stereotypes. Developmentally, AI companions and tutors shape how children learn and relate, prompting concerns about attachment and socialisation.
courses.description2: Explores philosophical foundations and implications of AI. Examines the history of AI, ethical issues like interpretability, bias and alignment, debates about AI consciousness and implications for human nature.
courses.topics: ai fairness; like interpretability; alignment; implications; human nature; consciousness
